newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-Individuals next in S.Africa forex control easing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Individuals next in S.Africa forex control easing.

text.p: Individuals should be the next to benefit from South Africa's gradual phasing out of foreign exchange controls, Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said on Tuesday.

Stals said he would advise the government that controls be relaxed to permit private individuals to take money out of the country, while at the same time special bonds were created to allow emigrants to access blocked funds over a number of years.
"I am keen to get a decision from the (finance) minister and the cabinet to do something for the private individual to enable him to make an investment outside the country," he told reporters.

Stals, speaking at a conference organised by stockbroker Societe Generale Frankel Pollak, said he would be holding serious discussions with Finance Minister Trevor Manuel on the matter over the next two or three weeks.
Manuel, who presents his 1997/98 budget to parliament on March 12, said at the same conference that remaining exchange controls would be phased out but he gave no details.
South Africa has already removed around 50 percent of its exchange controls, with institutions and companies granted increasing leeway to invest offshore.
Now the time has come to broaden the relaxation to individual members of the public, Stals said.
At present private individuals can invest in funds such as unit trusts which give them a limited exposure to overseas markets, but they are not allowed to take money out directly.
Relaxing controls in this area would provide the authorities with some measure of the demand among individuals to take money out -- and Stals said it might not turn out to be that great.

"My advice to most private individuals in South Africa will be: forget about it. Make an investment through an institutional investor if you want to, but you'll find over a longer term that the interest rates in South Africa are realistic enough to compensate you for exchange rate changes."

For emigrants, who have 10-15 billion rand ($2.26 - $3.39 billion) of funds blocked in South Africa, Stals said it made sense to offer a special non-resident bond which would free their cash gradually.

"What we are advising the government is to provide a bond that will become repayable and fully convertible after some years. We will make this available to former residents who will be able to invest at least part of their blocked funds in these bonds."

Stals said South Africa could hold a tender for say, 100 million rand ($22.5 million) of bonds, which would be available to non-residents at a set coupon, redeemable over perhaps five years in equal annual instalments.

"The government will have to decide on the conditions. But the broad principle is very easy, and it means that the government can borrow that money and use it for the time being as part of its budget financing," he said.
Expectations that South Africa will announce the next step in removing exchange controls, possibly around budget time, have been heightened by a strong rand and higher official reserves.

Stals agreed that the better market conditions this year made it easier to contemplate the next step in exchange control removal, but stressed once again that South Africa would not abolish all controls at once in a "big bang" move.
Foreign funds have flooded into South Africa this year and Stals said he expected capital inflows to jump to around 10 billion rand ($2.26 billion) in 1997 from 4.5 billion ($1.02 billion) in 1996.
